Probability and statistics OurBigBook.com

Probability plot

Words: 95
Statistics OurBigBook.com
A probability plot compares order statistics with plotting positions or model quantiles to diagnose whether a proposed probability distribution describes data. If the model can be transformed into a linear identity T(F(x))=a+bS(x), plot T(i/(n+1)) against S(X(i)​). Approximate linearity supports that model's shape; systematic curvature suggests a mismatch.
The plotting position i/(n+1) comes from the exact mean of the ith uniform order statistic, by the probability integral transform. It does not assert equality between the expectation of a nonlinear transformation and that transformation of the expectation. Fitted slope and intercept can estimate model parameters, but the visual plot alone is not a calibrated hypothesis test.

Relative frequency (fi​=ni​/n)

Words: 30
Statistics OurBigBook.com
For a sample or finite biological population of positive size n, the relative frequency of a category represented ni​ times is ni​/n. It is a proportion and differs from an oscillation frequency.

Descriptive statistics

Words: 2k Articles: 10
Probability and statistics OurBigBook.com
Descriptive statistics summarizes observed data, for example through location and spread statistics or graphical summaries such as a histogram.

Frequency table

Words: 150 Articles: 3
Descriptive statistics OurBigBook.com
A table of category counts, often accompanied by sample proportions or percentages. Its denominator must be stated, especially when observations contain missing data.

Expected frequency (Ej​=npj​)

Words: 61
Frequency table OurBigBook.com
The expected value of the number of observations in a category under a specified statistical model. For n observations with common category probability pj​, linearity of expectation gives Ej​=npj​; the calculation does not itself require independence. In a contingency table, fitting independence gives Eij​=ni+​n+j​/n. These are model-based counts, which may be fractional, rather than an additional set of observed responses. Pearson's chi-squared test compares observed counts with their corresponding expected frequencies.

Cumulative percentage

Words: 34
Frequency table OurBigBook.com
The sum of category percentages up to a specified position in an ordering. It has a substantive interpretation for an ordinal categorical variable; the cumulative percentage of an arbitrarily ordered nominal categorical variable changes when the labels are reordered.

Valid percentage

Words: 35
Frequency table OurBigBook.com
A percentage whose denominator excludes observations missing the variable being summarized. It can differ from a percentage calculated over the complete dataset's sample size. Valid percentages for two different variables need not use the same observations.

Mode (statistics)

Words: 67
Descriptive statistics OurBigBook.com
A mode is a value at which a probability mass function or specified probability density function attains its largest value. There may be more than one. For the normal distribution the unique mode equals the mean; the Maxwell speed distribution has mode 2kB​T/m​ and a larger mean speed. For a continuous probability distribution, a mode maximizes density rather than the probability of an exact value, which is zero. Density modes can change under a nonlinear change of variables, as the distinction between Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution and Maxwell speed distribution illustrates.

Scatter plot

Words: 36
Descriptive statistics OurBigBook.com
A scatter plot represents paired quantitative observations as points in a coordinate plane. Group labels, uncertainty and transformations can reveal nonlinear patterns or heterogeneous associations that a single correlation coefficient conceals. A visual association does not establish causation.

Box plot

Words: 478
Descriptive statistics OurBigBook.com
A box plot compresses a statistical sample into a box spanning its lower and upper quartiles Q1​,Q3​, a line at its median Q2​, and two whiskers. It makes location and central spread easy to compare across groups on a common value axis. The box represents the central half in terms of quantile levels; with ties or interpolated quartiles, it need not contain exactly half the observations. Whisker endpoints require a stated convention: they can be the observed extremes, or they can stop short of separately marked observations. [ref]
Here is one explicitly toy dataset, reused under histogram: twelve invented, unitless values, with repeated values counted separately, already arranged as order statistics:
(x(1)​,…,x(12)​)=(1,2,2,3,4,4,5,6,6,7,8,20).
(1)
For this box plot we choose the interpolated quartiles defined under quartile, using R's type-7 rule. This gives
Q1​=2+43​(3−2)=2.75,Q2​=4+21​(5−4)=4.5,Q3​=6+41​(7−6)=6.25.
(2)
The interquartile range is I=Q3​−Q1​=3.5. Our whisker convention uses the fences
L=Q1​−1.5I=−2.5,U=Q3​+1.5I=11.5.
(3)
The whiskers end at the smallest and largest observations in the closed interval [L,U]: here 1 and 8. Values strictly outside the fences receive separate outlier markers: here only 20. An observation exactly on a fence is retained within the whisker under this convention. The fences are thresholds, not observed whisker endpoints; the upper whisker is at 8, not 11.5. R's documented whisker rule likewise includes observations no more than 1.5 box lengths away, although its box uses hinges, which can differ from our type-7 quartiles. [ref]
A separate outlier marker is a prompt to investigate, not a finding that the value is bad data and not an instruction to delete it. A distant observation can be a recording error, a legitimate unusual outcome, or evidence that the assumed statistical model misses some behavior. Check its provenance and context before deciding how to analyze it. No measurement-error claim is possible for our invented 20: we deliberately put it there to demonstrate the rule. [ref]
The beauty of a box plot is its compact comparison of ordered positions rather than every observation. That compression also loses information: many different statistical samples have the same quartiles and whiskers, so the box alone cannot reveal every cluster or gap that a histogram might show. For example, replacing the two invented 6 values by 5.5 and 6 leaves the type-7 quartiles, whiskers and separate marker unchanged. Displaying the individual values alongside the box plot is especially helpful for such a small statistical sample. Always state both the quartile rule and the whisker rule; changing either can change which values are marked.

Quartile (Q1​,Q2​,Q3​)

Words: 171 Articles: 1
Descriptive statistics OurBigBook.com
Quartiles are the quantiles at probability levels 1/4,1/2,3/4; Q2​ is a median. For a population we can use its quantile function, Qr​=Q(r/4) for r=1,2,3. Finite-sample conventions differ. Our box plot uses linear interpolation between order statistics: for n≥2 and 0<p<1, set
h=1+(n−1)p,j=⌊h⌋,g=h−j,Q​(p)=(1−g)x(j)​+gx(j+1)​.
(4)
Then Qr​=Q​(r/4). This is R's type-7 convention, described in the documentation authored by Ivan Frohne and Rob J Hyndman. It differs from the generalized-inverse sample quantile defined elsewhere in this wiki: for the twelve toy values, that rule selects ranks 3,6,9 and gives 2,4,6, rather than 2.75,4.5,6.25. These are different stated conventions, not arithmetic disagreements. [ref]

Interquartile range (IQR=Q3​−Q1​)

Words: 61

The interquartile range measures the width between the lower and upper quartiles, in the same units as the observations. It describes central spread rather than the distance between the observed extremes. In our toy box plot, IQR=6.25−2.75=3.5; moving the largest value from 20 to 200 would leave the quartiles and interquartile range unchanged under the chosen rule, because the order statistics used in their interpolation would not change.

Histogram

Words: 630
Descriptive statistics OurBigBook.com
A histogram groups numerical observations into adjacent intervals called bins and draws one rectangle per bin. Its attraction is that a long list of values becomes a visible pattern of concentration, gaps and skewness. Specify the bin edges, the treatment of values on those edges, and what the vertical axis means: count, proportion, or density. Those choices are part of the graphic. [ref]
Let n>0 observations be covered by disjoint bins Bj​ with positive widths Δj​ and counts nj​, so ∑j​nj​=n. For example, use left-closed, right-open bins, closing the final right edge too. The three common height choices have different meanings:
  • Count height nj​ gives the number in bin j; the sum of heights is n.
  • Proportion height nj​/n gives the fraction in bin j; the sum of heights is 1.
  • Density height nj​/(nΔj​) makes the area, rather than the height, equal to the fraction in bin j.
For the density convention, a histogram is a piecewise constant probability density function estimate:
f​(x)=nΔj​nj​​(x∈Bj​),f​(x)=0(x∈/⋃j​Bj​).
(5)
Its normalization follows by adding rectangular areas:
∫Bj​​f​(x)dx=nnj​​,∫R​f​(x)dx=∑j​nnj​​=1.
(6)
If the observations have units, density has reciprocal units; a density height is not a probability and can exceed 1. With equal bin widths, count heights and density heights differ only by a common scale factor. With unequal widths, count-height areas nj​Δj​ give wider bins extra visual weight unrelated to their counts. Dividing by width removes that distortion. R's histogram documentation explicitly describes area-one normalization for unequal bins. [ref]
Reuse the twelve invented values under box plot, with bins [0,2),[2,4),[4,8),[8,22]. The counts are (1,3,6,2) and the widths are (2,2,4,14). Hence the density heights and areas are exactly
(241​,81​,81​,841​),(121​,41​,21​,61​).
(7)
The second and third bars have equal density heights even though the third contains twice as many observations: it is also twice as wide. The last bar contains only two observations; its count-height area would be 2⋅14=28, larger than the six-observation bar's 6⋅4=24. Its correct density area is only 1/6.
Bin choice trades detail against stability. Broad bins merge distinctions: the toy bin [8,22] hides the empty stretch between 8 and 20. Narrow bins expose gaps but can make each individual observation dominate a bar. With one-unit bins starting at 0, the bins [2,3),[4,5),[6,7) each contain two values and appear equally prominent; that apparent pattern depends on grouping the repeated integers together. Moving the bin origin also changes membership without changing the observations. For density estimation, this is a form of the bias-variance tradeoff: averaging over broad bins loses local detail, while narrow bins give more variable density estimates across repeated statistical samples. [ref] A useful practice is to compare a few plausible widths and offsets, keeping common edges when comparing groups. Automatic bin selectors are starting points, rather than guarantees of a unique correct picture. [ref]
A histogram retains only bin membership. Its density estimate spreads each bin's fraction uniformly across that bin, so our last bar assigns density throughout [8,22] even though the only toy values there are 8 and 20. It does not recover within-bin positions or observation order, and a visually convincing shape does not establish a population probability distribution. A box plot provides a complementary compact summary of quartiles; neither graphic replaces the original observations.

Birthday problem (Pn,m​=1−∏j=0n−1​(1−j/m))

Words: 754 Articles: 4
Probability and statistics OurBigBook.com
The birthday problem asks for the probability that at least two members of a group share a birthday. Use the explicit model of independent random variables taking m labels with a uniform distribution on a finite set. Let m≥1 and n≥0 be integers. For calendar examples below, stipulate m=365 equally likely labels and omit leap days. For 0≤n≤m, the probability of at least one matching pair is
Pn,m​=1−mnm(m−1)⋯(m−n+1)​=1−j=0∏n−1​(1−mj​).​
(8)
At n=0, the empty product is one and P0,m​=0. At n>m, a repeat is certain by the pigeonhole principle. Count the complement to obtain the formula: the first label has m choices, then a distinct second label has m−1, and so forth, out of mn equally likely label sequences.[ref]
For the stipulated calendar, P22,365​≈47.57% and P23,365​≈50.73%. Only 23 people suffice to put the probability above one half. There are (223​)=253 possible pairs, each with matching probability 1/365. The many comparison opportunities explain why a small group can contain a repeat.
The distinction also matters for hash collisions. If independently generated outputs of a hash function are uniformly distributed over m possible labels, the same counting formula governs repeats. The birthday square-root scale explains why looking for any repeated output requires far fewer labels than trying to match one predetermined output. The uniform-independent model is an assumption about those outputs; the birthday problem does not itself establish that a particular implementation meets it.

Matching one specified birthday (1−(1−1/m)n−1)

Words: 157
Birthday problem OurBigBook.com
In a group of total size n≥1, designate one member and ask whether any of the other n−1 labels equals that member's label. Conditional on the designated label, all the other draws avoid it with probability 1−1/m. Independence gives
P(a match with the designated member)=1−(1−m1​)n−1.​
(9)
For n=23, this is approximately 5.86%, while the probability of some matching pair is approximately 50.73%. The designated-member question examines 22 pairs; the any-pair question examines all 253. A repeated label elsewhere in the group does not require a match with its designated member.

Birthday collision count (C=∑i<j​1{Xi​=Xj​}​,E[C]=(2n​)/m)

Birthday problem OurBigBook.com
The birthday collision count counts equal-label unordered pairs. Write it as a sum of indicator random variables:
C=∑1≤i<j≤n​1{Xi​=Xj​}​,E[C]=∑i<j​m1​=2mn(n−1)​.
(10)
This uses linearity of expectation; mutual independence of the pair indicators is unnecessary. For 23 uniform calendar labels, E[C]=253/365≈0.69315, whereas P(C≥1)≈0.50730. A configuration with three equal labels contributes three pairs, so counting pairs and recording whether any pair exists are different random variables.
Treating every pair event as mutually independent would give the wrong exact formula. For three draws, X1​=X2​ and X1​=X3​ force X2​=X3​. The probability that all three equalities hold is 1/m2, while the product of their individual probabilities is 1/m3 for m>1. This distinguishes independence of the original label draws from mutual independence of events built from overlapping draws.

Birthday square-root scale (n≍m​)

Words: 111
Birthday problem OurBigBook.com
The union bound gives Pn,m​≤min(1,n(n−1)/(2m)). Using 1−x≤e−x on the distinct-label product gives
1−e−n(n−1)/(2m)≤Pn,m​≤min(1,2mn(n−1)​).
(11)
The lower bound reaches at least one half when n(n−1)/(2m)≥log2. The simple approximation n≈2mlog2​ predicts a group size near 23 for m=365. It is the quadratic number of pairs that makes the square root appear.
For a precise limiting statement, let m→∞ and n/m​→c≥0. Expanding the logarithm of the complement yields
log(1−Pn,m​)=−2mn(n−1)​+O(m2n3​),Pn,m​⟶1−e−c2/2.
(12)
On this scale the remainder tends to zero. Thus a fixed substantial collision probability appears after order m​ draws. For m=2b uniform output labels, the corresponding scale is order 2b/2; matching one specified birthday instead involves a number of draws of order m.

For the original chosen probabilities (1/2,1/4,1/8,1/8), this is 11/32=0.34375, rather than the uniform four-label value 1/4. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives 1=(∑i​pi​)2≤m∑i​pi2​, so uniform probabilities minimize this two-draw collision probability. Q-Q plot

Words: 869 Articles: 2
Probability and statistics OurBigBook.com
A Q-Q plot is a scatter plot pairing quantiles at the same probability levels. For a statistical sample of size n, sort the observations into order statistics x(1)​≤⋯≤x(n)​. Choose plotting positions pi​ and a reference quantile function Q0​, then plot
(Q0​(pi​),x(i)​),pi​=ni−1/2​,i=1,…,n.
(14)
Here the horizontal coordinate is a reference value, and the vertical coordinate is an observed value; neither axis is the probability pi​. The displayed plotting positions are our chosen convention, placing every level strictly between zero and one. They are not a claim that the ith order statistic equals that population quantile. For two statistical samples, use sample quantiles at matching levels, with a stated interpolation convention when their sizes differ. [ref]
As a computed example, take n=19 and the standard normal quantiles zi​=Φ−1(pi​), where Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. Construct the ordered values ai​=10+2zi​. At ranks 1,10,19, the plotting positions are 1/38,1/2,37/38, the reference quantiles are approximately −1.937932,0,1.937932, and the constructed values are approximately 6.124137,10,13.875863. Every point lies on a=10+2z by construction. These 19 values are deliberately chosen, not random draws or real measurements.
The usefulness of a Q-Q plot is that it turns a comparison of probability distributions into geometry: if a reference random variable Z is transformed into X=μ+σZ with σ>0, its quantile function satisfies QX​(p)=μ+σQZ​(p). This follows because a positive scaling preserves ordering. Thus the location-scale family produces a straight population Q-Q plot, and an approximate sample line suggests a compatible shape over the observed range. Its intercept describes location and its slope describes scale. The identity line requires the same location, scale and units on both axes; even then its displayed angle is 45 degrees only with equal axis scales. Curvature is often more informative than a histogram because it shows which quantiles depart from the reference. [ref]

Normal Q-Q plot

Words: 459
Q-Q plot OurBigBook.com
A normal Q-Q plot compares order statistics with standard normal quantiles zi​=Φ−1(pi​). For a normal distribution N(μ,σ2) with σ>0, the population quantile function is μ+σΦ−1(p), so the diagnostic sample relation is
x(i)​≈μ+σzi​.
(15)
The appropriate reference is a line with an intercept and positive slope, not necessarily the identity line. A line can be fitted through two central sample quantiles; R's qqline uses the quantile levels p=0.25 and p=0.75 by default. Neither that line nor its fitting rule is part of the definition of a normal Q-Q plot. [ref]
To isolate curvature, retain the same 19 plotting positions and construct two more ordered sequences:
bi​=2pi​−1,ci​=sinh(0.7zi​).
(16)
The bi​ are continuous uniform distribution quantiles on [−1,1], while the ci​ apply the hyperbolic sine to the reference quantiles. Both examples are symmetric about zero. At ranks 1,10,19, bi​ is approximately −0.947368,0,0.947368 and ci​ is approximately −1.812618,0,1.812618. Again, these are constructed values rather than random draws or real data.
Read these shapes relative to their central slope. The uniform distribution example has b(z)=2Φ(z)−1, with derivative b′(0)=2/π​≈0.797885; at the upper endpoint the tangent predicts 1.546246, while b19​=0.947368. Its lower end lies above the tangent and its upper end below it: the outer quantiles are compressed. The hyperbolic sine example has c′(0)=0.7; its tangent predicts 1.356552 at the upper endpoint, while c19​=1.812618. Its lower end lies below the tangent and its upper end above it: the outer quantiles are stretched. Unequal departures at the two ends can suggest skewness. The direction of these descriptions assumes that reference quantiles are horizontal and observed values vertical. The graphs illustrate finite-range shape differences; a sample pattern cannot establish an asymptotic tail probability law or membership in a heavy-tailed distribution class.
A nearly straight normal Q-Q plot is a diagnostic, not a proof of a normal distribution or a formal hypothesis test. Random statistical samples fluctuate, particularly at extreme order statistics, and apparent curvature depends on sample size, plotting positions and the reference line. A calibrated hypothesis test or uncertainty band requires its own assumptions and must account for parameters estimated from the same observations. Sorting also discards the original observation order: rearranging a time series leaves its Q-Q plot unchanged, so the plot cannot establish independence.
For a normal linear model, R's diagnostic normal Q-Q plot uses standardized regression residuals, also called internally studentized residuals. [ref] Even with independent errors, the regression residuals have covariance matrix σ2(I−H), where H is the hat matrix; fitting parameters generally creates dependencies. Dividing by a shared estimated standard deviation creates further dependence, and the distribution of an internally studentized Gaussian residual is not exactly the standard normal distribution. The normal Q-Q plot therefore helps assess error shape alongside other diagnostics rather than certifying independent normal random variables.

Change-point detection estimates locations where a sequence's distribution or mean changes. A piecewise-constant mean has a sparse vector of adjacent differences; one-dimensional total variation denoising exploits this sparsity without fixing the number of changes in advance.

Poisson count change-point model with gamma priors (p(λ,ϕ,m∣x)∝λα+Sm​−1e−(β+m)λϕγ+SN​−Sm​−1e−(δ+N−m)ϕ)

Change-point detection OurBigBook.com
For independent Poisson distributions with rate λ up to an unknown index m and rate ϕ after it, independent shape-rate Gamma distribution priors give the displayed posterior distribution when m is uniform on {1,…,N} and Sm​=∑i≤m​xi​. The model differs from a continuous-time Poisson change-point posterior. The endpoint m=N represents no observed change: the second segment is empty and its rate keeps its prior law.

Marginal posterior weights of a Poisson count change point (wm​=(β+m)α+Sm​(δ+N−m)γ+SN​−Sm​Γ(α+Sm​)Γ(γ+SN​−Sm​)​)

Words: 61
Poisson count change-point model with gamma priors OurBigBook.com
Integrating the two rates out of the Poisson count change-point model with gamma priors gives these weights up to a common factor, by the defining Gamma function integral. Normalizing across the finitely many possible indices gives the exact marginal posterior distribution of m, providing a check on Markov chain Monte Carlo estimates. One can also draw m from these weights and then draw both rates from their conditional Gamma distributions, producing independent exact joint posterior samples.

Gibbs updates for a Poisson count change point

Words: 55
Poisson count change-point model with gamma priors OurBigBook.com
The full conditional distributions are λ∣m,x∼Gamma(α+Sm​,β+m) and ϕ∣m,x∼Gamma(γ+SN​−Sm​,δ+N−m), in shape-rate notation. Conditional on the two rates, m has weights wj​=exp[j(ϕ−λ)+Sj​log(λ/ϕ)]. A Gibbs sampler cycles through these three draws. Each update preserves the joint posterior distribution; subtracting the largest log weight before exponentiation stabilizes the categorical draw. Averages of 1{m=N}​ estimate the posterior probability of no observed change.

Take independent proper normal prior distributions for the two segment means and a proper inverse-gamma distribution for the common variance. A uniform prior distribution over m=1,…,n may then retain the empty second segment. The posterior distribution is proper: its likelihood function is bounded above by (2π)−n/2v−n/2, whose integral against IG(a0​,b0​) is finite for a0​,b0​>0. At m=n the second mean has its unchanged proper prior distribution as its full conditional distribution. The configuration's posterior probability now has the meaningful interpretation of no change inside the observed sample.

For independent means θ∼N(μθ​,tθ​) and ϕ∼N(μϕ​,tϕ​), the first mean's conditional precision is m/v+1/tθ​ and conditional precision-weighted mean is ∑i≤m​xi​/v+μθ​/tθ​; replace m by n−m for the second mean. With v∼IG(a0​,b0​) its conditional law is IG(a0​+n/2,b0​+Sm​/2). The discrete split has conditional probabilities proportional to e−Sm​/(2v). These full conditional distributions give a Gibbs sampler including m=n. Averaging the sampled indicators of that configuration estimates its probability; averaging its conditional probabilities gives an estimate by Rao-Blackwellization.

Measurement error is the difference between a recorded variable and the quantity it is intended to measure. It can attenuate associations, create misclassification, and bias nonlinear estimators even when the error has mean zero.

Measurement error OurBigBook.com
A component of measurement error fluctuating between repetitions under specified conditions, as distinguished from a shared systematic error. Independent zero-mean fluctuations of variance σ2 give a sample-mean variance σ2/N; correlated fluctuations need not follow this averaging law.

Measurement noise (n(t))

Words: 58
Measurement error OurBigBook.com
Measurement noise is a fluctuating contribution to measurement error. An additive model for a measured output is ym​(t)=y(t)+n(t), where y is the actual plant output. A controller using feedback control can react to n as though it were a change in the plant output. This effect is absent from the ideal noiseless examples under control theory; an errors-in-variables model represents a related distinction between latent quantities and their noisy observations.

Errors-in-variables model

Words: 64
Measurement error OurBigBook.com
An errors-in-variables model distinguishes a latent true predictor from its noisy measurement and models both the measurement and the response. For example, Wi​∣Ui​∼N(Ui​,s2) and Yi​∣Ui​∼N(a+bUi​,v2), with a population distribution for Ui​, propagate predictor uncertainty into inference on b. Treating Wi​ as exact can create attenuation bias from classical measurement error. Identifiability requires appropriate information about the measurement process or latent predictor distribution.

Regression toward the mean

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Probability and statistics OurBigBook.com
Regression toward the mean is a tendency for measurements selected because they are extreme to be less extreme on repetition. A large first reading can combine a persistent signal with unusually positive measurement error; a fresh error need not repeat that contribution. This can change the selected group's mean even when the underlying signal stays fixed and no intervention occurs.
The claim concerns a conditional expectation, not a rule that every individual moves toward the population mean. Some second readings are more extreme. Nor does an observed change establish a causal effect: selection alone can produce it. The following original normal distribution model makes both distinctions quantitative.

Repeated-measurement latent signal model (X=T+ε1​,Y=T+ε2​)

Words: 640 Articles: 2
Regression toward the mean OurBigBook.com
Imagine an instrument measuring the same fixed quantity twice on each unit. Across units the persistent signal T is a latent variable; the two measurement errors ε1​,ε2​ are fresh, mutually independent random variables, also independent of T. Assume they have mean zero and common finite variance v, while T has mean μ and variance s. Then
X=T+ε1​,Y=T+ε2​,E[X]=E[Y]=μ,Var(X)=Var(Y)=s+v,Cov(X,Y)=s.
(18)
Thus the Pearson correlation coefficient is ρ=s/(s+v) when s+v>0. Both measurements retain the same marginal mean and variance. Repetition does not make the entire population collapse toward μ; it changes what we expect after selecting on X.
For s,v>0, further assuming normal distributions for T and both measurement errors gives the conditional expectation
E[Y∣X=x]=μ+ρ(x−μ).
(19)
Since 0<ρ<1, this predicted reading is closer to μ than x is. Independence and zero mean errors alone do not justify this linear conditional expectation: without the normal distribution assumption the same expression is the linear least-squares projection, and the actual conditional expectation can be nonlinear. Correlated errors, a changing signal, or different error variances require their own model; a noisy reading by itself supplies no universal shrinkage factor.

Gaussian regression toward the mean (Y∣X=x∼N(0.6x,0.64))

Words: 472 Articles: 1
Repeated-measurement latent signal model OurBigBook.com
Take the original synthetic model T∼N(0,0.6) and ε1​,ε2​∼N(0,0.4), mutually independent random variables, with the second argument denoting variance. The pair (X,Y) has a multivariate normal distribution with mean zero, unit marginal variances, and Pearson correlation coefficient 0.6. Its conditional multivariate normal distribution is
Y∣X=x∼N(0.6x,1−0.62)=N(0.6x,0.64).
(20)
For a first reading x=2, the second reading has conditional expectation 1.2 and conditional variance 0.64, hence standard deviation 0.8. There is still conditional probability 1−Φ(1)≈0.1587 of Y>2, a movement farther from zero, where Φ is the standard normal distribution function. The line 0.6x describes a conditional mean, not an individual trajectory.
A short derivation isolates R=Y−0.6X. Its covariance with X is zero and its variance is 0.64. Because (X,R) has a multivariate normal distribution, zero covariance implies independence: R∼N(0,0.64) independently of X. This also explains why reversing the two measurements gives E[X∣Y=y]=0.6y. The statistical association does not identify a direction of causal effect.

E[T∣X>1]≈0.915081,E[ε1​∣X>1]≈0.610054,E[ε2​∣X>1]=0.

The first measurement error has zero unconditional mean, but positive selected mean. The second measurement error stays centered because it is independent of selection on X. The persistent signal T never changed.

Regression toward the mean and randomized comparisons

Words: 195
Regression toward the mean OurBigBook.com
For causal inference, a before-and-after change among units selected by an extreme baseline reading combines any causal effect with the change expected from selection. In the synthetic model the selected-group mean falls by about 0.610 with no intervention at all. Calling that entire fall an intervention effect would attribute a predictable measurement error contribution to a change in the signal.
One comparison design selects all eligible units by the same rule, then uses randomization to assign an intervention or a comparison condition, with the same measurement times and instrument in both groups. To see the principle algebraically, let assignment A∈{0,1} be independent of (T,ε1​,ε2​) within the selected population, and let the intervention add a constant δ to the second reading: Y=T+ε2​+δA. Then
E[Y−X∣X>1,A=1]=−0.610054…+δ,E[Y−X∣X>1,A=0]=−0.610054….
(24)
Subtracting the two expected changes isolates δ under these assumptions. Both groups experience the same selection tendency in expectation. A finite experiment still has sampling uncertainty; randomization does not guarantee identical realized groups. Without randomization, the same threshold alone does not establish comparable latent signals or error processes. Different selection rules, selective follow-up, changing instruments, or common temporal changes also require explicit assumptions. This is a statistical inference principle about comparisons, not evidence that any particular intervention works.

Galton's stature regression

Words: 156
Regression toward the mean OurBigBook.com
Francis Galton's paper Regression towards mediocrity in hereditary stature by Francis Galton analyzes adult offspring heights against the average of their parents' adjusted heights. He multiplied female heights by 1.08 before making that parental average. Table I contains 928 adult offspring from 205 parental pairs; the opening prose instead states 930. Its grouped readout is a median, and the explanation of Plate IX describes a smoothed offspring deviation about two-thirds of the parental deviation.[ref]
These were parent-offspring records, not repeat readings of an unchanged signal. The paper's group tendency does not say that every child must be closer to the population mean. Galton also reports uncertainty over whether some recorded heights included shoes, a concrete measurement error limitation.[ref] The 0.6 Pearson correlation coefficient and all generated values above are our chosen model, not a reconstruction of his data.

Without reflection symmetry an additional antisymmetric, helical term can occur.

A random field is statistically homogeneous when all of its joint distributions are invariant under a common spatial translation of their arguments. Its momentum-space correlation functions consequently contain a Dirac delta function imposing total-momentum conservation.

Missing data

Words: 1k Articles: 28
Probability and statistics OurBigBook.com
Missing data occur when some intended measurements are unobserved. Whether valid inference can ignore the missingness mechanism depends on how the probability of observation relates to observed and unobserved values.

Missingness overlap from marginal and complete-case counts (mXY​=mX​+mY​−(N−nXY​))

Words: 128
Missing data OurBigBook.com
For N observations, let mX​ and mY​ count missing values of two variables, and let nXY​ count observations on which both are available. The number missing at least one variable is N−nXY​. Applying the inclusion-exclusion principle to the two missing-value sets gives the displayed number missing both. The disjoint counts are consequently mX​−mXY​ missing only X, mY​−mXY​ missing only Y, mXY​ missing both, and nXY​ complete cases. Their nonnegativity is a necessary consistency check on the supplied totals.
This identifies an aggregate missingness pattern without reconstructing individual records. It does not identify a missing-data mechanism, establish missing completely at random, or justify treating a substantive response such as an explicit unknown category as a missing observation. Counts from different cohorts cannot be inserted into the identity without first establishing a common denominator.

Observed-case analysis

Words: 26
Missing data OurBigBook.com
An analysis restricted to cases with an observed endpoint. Its result need not describe the whole eligible cohort when observation depends on outcome or related characteristics.

Words: 94
Missing data OurBigBook.com
Suppose an endpoint is binary, N people are in the target cohort, r observed outcomes are successes and m outcomes are missing. With no assumptions about the missing values, the cohort success proportion p satisfies
Nr​≤p≤Nr+m​.
(27)
For the proof, let u be the number of successes among the missing outcomes. Since 0≤u≤m and p=(r+u)/N, both inequalities follow. Every integer u in that range is a possible completion of the observed data, so the endpoints are sharp. These are missing data bounds on a cohort proportion, not confidence intervals or bounds on a causal treatment effect.

Words: 112 Articles: 1
Missing data OurBigBook.com
Item nonresponse leaves a particular measurement unobserved while retaining other measurements on that individual. Unit nonresponse leaves all survey measurements unavailable. Adjusting for an observed auxiliary variable can address item nonresponse under missing at random, but does not identify the auxiliary-variable distribution among unit nonresponders. Extrapolation to them needs further assumptions or external information.

Words: 60
Unit and item nonresponse OurBigBook.com
Vary the unobserved outcome probabilities for item and unit nonresponders, and any unknown auxiliary-variable mixture, over scientifically plausible ranges. Recompute the population estimate and identify values at which substantive conclusions change. This probes untestable transport or missing at random assumptions; it is distinct from sampling uncertainty represented by a confidence interval. Letting each missing-outcome probability vary from zero to one gives worst-case identification bounds.

Missing data OurBigBook.com
The mechanism assigns probabilities to observation patterns R conditional on complete measurements D: p(R∣D). Whether it depends on missing values distinguishes missing completely at random, missing at random and missing not at random.

Missingness depends only on fully observed covariates X, not on the response after conditioning on them. A responder-only marginal estimate may still be biased when response rates and outcome probabilities both vary across covariate strata. MAR standardization over a fully observed covariate weights within-stratum respondent estimates using covariate frequencies from the whole target cohort.

For A=m, the unobserved outcome is integrated out, giving ∫fβ​(y)∏j=1m​qj​(y)dy. These probabilities sum to one by telescoping and integration. Dependence of qj​ on y models missing not at random. If all qj​ are independent of y conditional on the regression predictors, the outcome density among responders remains fβ​, as required for complete-case analysis of that conditional model.

Data are missing completely at random when the missingness indicator is independent of both observed and missing data.

With a fully observed covariate X, response Y, and an independent response indicator with probability ρ, let m(X)=E(Y∣X). A covariate-standardized mean has asymptotic variance [Var(m)+E{Var(Y∣X)}/ρ]/N, whereas the complete-case mean has variance Var(Y)/(Nρ). The difference is (1−ρ)Var(m)/(Nρ). Thus missing completely at random does not justify discarding predictive observed covariates on efficiency grounds.

Missing data OurBigBook.com
Data are missing at random when the probability of missingness, conditional on observed data, does not depend further on the missing values.

For each fixed observation pattern, the probability of that pattern may depend on observed response components and fully observed covariates, but not on the response components missing under that pattern. When a response Y is missing at random conditional on a fully observed category X, estimate its conditional probabilities using respondents within each category and average them with the category frequencies from all patients. For a binary response, P(Y=1)=∑x​P(X=x)P(Y=1∣X=x,R=1). The weighting uses the full cohort rather than only complete cases.

A missingness mechanism is ignorable for likelihood or Bayesian inference about outcome-model parameters when the missingness-model factor can be omitted without changing that inference. Missing at random together with distinct outcome and missingness parameters is a standard sufficient condition.

If a regression response Y is observed but covariate X is sometimes missing, likelihood inference requires a joint model: for example fβ​(y∣x)gη​(x). An incomplete record contributes ∫fβ​(y∣x)gη​(x)dx to the observed-data likelihood. Missing data OurBigBook.com
Data are missing not at random when the probability of missingness still depends on an unobserved value after conditioning on the observed data.

Model the joint distribution by multiplying a response model by a sequential dropout model. For example, the logit of dropout before visit j, conditional on remaining observed, can depend on the currently unobserved Yij​ as well as previous responses and baseline covariates. The observed-data likelihood sums over the missing binary responses. Such a dependence parameter is usually weakly identified or unidentified from observed responses alone; sensitivity analysis must vary it over scientifically justified values.

A response model and a dropout model share latent random effects. Conditional on those effects and observed predictors, the two processes may be independent, yet marginally dropout is missing not at random because the shared effects also predict unseen outcomes. Joint likelihood fitting integrates the product of both models over the shared effects; integrating the outcome model alone is insufficient. This is an explicit identifying model, and its latent-dependence assumptions should be assessed by sensitivity analysis.

Repeated measurements have a monotone missing-data pattern when every measurement after a subject's first missing value is also missing.

A complete-case analysis uses only observations for which every variable required by the analysis is observed. It can be biased when completeness selects observations according to their outcomes or other relevant variables.

Suppose N>d≥0 observations lie in [a,b] and have sample mean yˉ​. Delete any d observations. The remaining sample mean obeys
N−dNyˉ​−db​≤yˉ​remaining​≤N−dNyˉ​−da​.

Indeed, the removed sum is between da and db; subtract it from the original sum Nyˉ​ and divide by the remaining positive count. This does not justify the unadjusted complete-case mean when observation rates and outcome means both vary with X, nor does it imply missing completely at random.

A recorded variable included in imputation models to help predict missing values or explain response patterns, even if it is absent from the final substantive model. Use the pooled estimate and total variance from Rubin's rules. A basic large-complete-sample scalar interval is Q​±tν,1−α/2​T​, with ν=(M−1)[1+U/((1+M−1)B)]2 for B>0. Specify a conditional distribution for each incomplete variable given the others, cycle through parameter draws and missing-value draws, and retain multiple completed datasets after suitable convergence checks. A trial designed to estimate an intervention's effects under circumstances relevant to ordinary clinical delivery. Generalisability still depends on recruitment, setting, comparator and implementation.

Clinical trial OurBigBook.com
An incremental effect relative to a specified comparison intended to address an alternative explanation. A package effect beyond waiting, a benefit beyond credible contact and a causal component mechanism are different levels of specificity.

Clinical trial OurBigBook.com
Expectation that an intervention will help. It is distinct from actual benefit and from credibility of the proposed explanation.

Clinical trial OurBigBook.com
How plausible and relevant a treatment appears to participants. Contact-matched interventions need not produce equal credibility or expectations, so these influences should be measured.

Clinical trial OurBigBook.com
An effect attributed to influences shared across interventions, such as attention or expectations, relative to the mechanism under investigation. Shared does not mean inert, and matching session counts does not establish that every such influence is controlled.

Clinical trial OurBigBook.com
A specified health, symptom or functional endpoint assessed at a stated time. A symptom change, dimensional belief score and categorical recovery decision answer different clinical questions.

Meeting an explicitly specified recovery criterion in a clinical context. The criterion can concern symptoms, diagnosis or functioning; published recovery percentages cannot be interpreted without knowing that definition, timing and denominator.

Clinical trial OurBigBook.com
A comparator intended to lack a specified active treatment ingredient. Its credibility, expectations and contact still require assessment; a pill placebo is not automatically a contact-matched control for psychotherapy.

A therapist's preference, training or investment in a treatment approach. Unequal competence or expectations across trial arms can complicate a comparison of therapeutic models.

Clinical trial OurBigBook.com
The prespecified principal endpoint used to evaluate a trial's main hypothesis. Its measurement, assessment time and analysis population should be fixed before outcomes are inspected.

Words: 31
Clinical trial OurBigBook.com
Variation in the treatment effect with a baseline characteristic. An interaction tests differences in treatment effects; significance in one subgroup and nonsignificance in another is not itself evidence for an interaction.

Words: 77 Articles: 1
Clinical trial OurBigBook.com
A trial testing whether an intervention is no worse than a comparator by more than a prespecified clinically justified margin. For a higher-is-better outcome and difference d, a lower confidence bound above −Δ supports the stated margin. Failure of a superiority test is not sufficient; fidelity, attrition and intention-to-treat and sensitivity analyses affect interpretation.

Noninferiority margin (Δ)

Noninferiority trial OurBigBook.com
The maximum clinically acceptable disadvantage specified before seeing results. Its justification and the direction of a favourable outcome must be explicit.

Clinical trial OurBigBook.com
A randomised comparison that varies a specified treatment component while keeping the surrounding intervention appropriately similar. It is designed to separate component effects that cannot be inferred from efficacy of a multicomponent package.

Clinical trial OurBigBook.com
How participants experience and evaluate an intervention's procedures, burden and fit. High efficacy among completers does not establish acceptability among those who declined or discontinued.

Clinical trial OurBigBook.com
No longer meeting a specified diagnostic criterion at a stated assessment. Remission of the principal diagnosis, remission of every anxiety disorder, global improvement and symptom-score change must be reported separately.

Words: 40
Clinical trial OurBigBook.com
Adding an intervention to an existing treatment. To identify an incremental effect, comparison groups should share an adequate base treatment and match relevant contact or expectancy where possible. Benefit from the base treatment does not establish benefit from the addition.

Clinical trial OurBigBook.com
Independent trial safety monitoring reviews accumulating serious outcomes according to a prespecified plan and may recommend stopping or modifying a clinical trial when harm or benefit changes the ethical balance. Pooled evidence and prespecified sequential thresholds can make rare-event monitoring useful without presenting a nonsignificant harm comparison as safety.

Words: 56
Clinical trial OurBigBook.com
Clinical equipoise is genuine professional uncertainty about the relative overall benefit and harm of the treatments being compared in a randomized controlled trial. A favorable intermediate endpoint does not by itself resolve uncertainty about mortality. Ethical design requires informed consent, meaningful benefit-risk assessment and monitoring of serious harms; an underpowered safety comparison is not evidence that harm is absent.

Clinical trial OurBigBook.com
A clinical trial comparison must define a common time origin and observation window for both assigned treatments. A probability measured from allocation cannot be replaced by one measured from a later treatment-dependent release or discharge. The latter may describe a different time interval and a selected population. A numerical sample size cannot be obtained by silently treating those probabilities as interchangeable.

Clinical trial OurBigBook.com
Eligibility criteria specify which individuals may enter a clinical trial, defining its enrolled population and excluding individuals for whom the intervention or measurements are unsuitable. Screening applies those criteria before randomization. The treatment comparison's external validity depends on how this population relates to the population of interest.

A futility boundary specifies an interim result below which a clinical trial stops without rejecting the null hypothesis. Removing only potential rejection paths cannot increase the type I error. With a finite boundary and a nonsingular joint normal test-statistic distribution, it strictly reduces that error relative to the corresponding fixed-final-boundary test.

With stage standard error s, mean parameter δ, and combined mean S, the estimator bias after continuation is E(S∣X≥c)−δ=(s/2)λ((c−δ)/s), where λ is the upper-tail Inverse Mills ratio. It is positive and tends to zero as continuation becomes virtually certain.

The root is unique when the pooled stage-1 weight satisfies 0<w<1, because its conditional-mean map has derivative between 1−w and one. Coupling

Words: 1k Articles: 22
Probability and statistics OurBigBook.com
A coupling of probability distributions μ,ν is a joint probability distribution of random variables (X,Y) whose marginal distributions are μ,ν. It lets us choose the statistical dependence between two random constructions while preserving the individual laws. This choice can make a comparison much easier: giving two simulations the same random input may keep their paths close, even though separately generating both paths would hide that relationship.[ref]
For example, two fair coin tosses can be generated independently, with mismatch probability 1/2, or by tossing once and setting Y=X, with mismatch probability zero. Both constructions have the same two Bernoulli distributions as marginals. Their joint laws differ. A maximal coupling makes the values agree as often as possible; a coalescing coupling arranges permanent agreement of two processes after a random time. Minimizing expected geometric separation instead leads to Wasserstein distance.

Its chance of never resetting is ∏r≥0​(1−br​)>0. Successive failed attempts therefore end almost surely, leaving a final infinite run of matches. The dominating chain does not depend on the histories, so future-block laws forget the remote past uniformly. This proves uniqueness of a two-sided law with the prescribed transition kernel without assuming stationarity first.

One quantity connects probability bookkeeping, comparison of sampling methods, and the limits of a statistical test.

The event E={A} attains this difference: P(E)=0.4 and Q(E)=0.1. Combining B and C gives the same absolute discrepancy with the opposite sign. Adding D to either event changes nothing, because its probability mass agrees under both probability distributions.
The factor 1/2 is necessary because ∑x​(P(x)−Q(x))=0: every unit of excess probability mass must match a unit of deficit. For any event, including a negative term cannot increase its signed discrepancy, while omitting a positive term cannot increase it either. Therefore {x:P(x)>Q(x)} attains the positive maximum. This is a short way to compute an apparent optimization over 2∣S∣ subsets using one pass through S.
For probability density functions p,q relative to the same measure λ, the corresponding identity is dTV​(P,Q)=21​∫∣p−q∣dλ. Such densities can always be taken as Radon-Nikodym derivatives relative to λ=P+Q. Beware the notation: the total variation norm of a measure applied to the signed measure P−Q equals 2dTV​(P,Q). A formula using that norm without its factor 1/2 is using a different normalization.

The best success probability is 65%, with a 35% error probability. A smaller total variation distance means the two sources are harder to distinguish from one observation. Unequal prior probabilities, unequal costs, or multiple observations change this particular decision problem; the 65% figure is not a universal bound for every experiment.

Probability and statistics OurBigBook.com
A statistic T=T(X) is sufficient for a statistical model {Pθ​:θ∈Θ} when the conditional distribution of the full data X given T has a version independent of the unknown statistical parameter θ. Once T is recorded, the remaining uncertainty about the data's arrangement can be generated without knowing θ. [ref]
For data and statistic taking values in standard Borel spaces, express this precisely with one Markov kernel K, common to every statistical parameter value:
Pθ​(X∈B∣T)=K(T,B)Pθ​-almost surely,θ∈Θ,
(61)
for each measurable event B. Thus K(t,⋅) is a regular conditional distribution of X given T=t. Equality is only required outside a null set for the distribution of T under each θ; the choice of version matters on impossible conditioning events. For a continuous probability distribution, the event T=t may have zero probability even at meaningful observations, so the definition uses a regular conditional distribution, rather than division by Pθ​(T=t).
A sufficient statistic is a property of a specified statistical model, rather than of a formula for summarizing data in isolation. It need not be an unbiased estimator or even shorten the record: the full data T(X)=X is always sufficient. An estimator instead targets a quantity such as a mean. An ancillary statistic has a parameter-independent marginal probability distribution, whereas a sufficient statistic has a parameter-independent conditional full-data law. A minimal sufficient statistic permits the greatest reduction among sufficient statistics. A complete statistic satisfies a separate condition about zero expectations; a complete sufficient statistic must satisfy both conditions.

Bernoulli sample sum as a sufficient statistic (T=∑i=1n​Xi​)

Words: 386
Sufficient statistic OurBigBook.com
Let n be fixed and known, and let X1​,…,Xn​ be independent and identically distributed Bernoulli random variables with common success probability p. Their joint probability mass function, on the binary sample space {0,1}n, is
Pp​(X=x)=∏i=1n​pxi​(1−p)1−xi​=pt(1−p)n−t,t=T(x)=∑i=1n​xi​.
(62)
There are (tn​) arrangements with t successes, so T has the binomial distribution. For 0<p<1 and t∈{0,…,n}, its exact conditional full-data probability mass function is
Pp​(X=x∣T=t)=(tn​)pt(1−p)n−tpt(1−p)n−t1{T(x)=t}​​=(tn​)1{T(x)=t}​​.
(63)
This conditional distribution is uniform over arrangements, with no dependence on p: the sum is a sufficient statistic. [ref]
For n=4, the group sizes are 1,4,6,4,1 and the within-group conditional probabilities are respectively 1,1/4,1/6,1/4,1. For example, T=2 leaves exactly 0011,0101,0110,1001,1010,1100, each with conditional probability 1/6. At p=1/4, each such sequence has unconditional probability 9/256 and the group has probability 54/256. At p=1/2, these values are 1/16 and 6/16; at p=3/4 they return to 9/256 and 54/256. The conditional weights stay 1/6 in all three cases.
At the boundary p=0, only T=0 has positive probability; at p=1, only T=n does. Dividing by Pp​(T=t) on the other groups would divide by zero. Nevertheless, the same uniform-on-arrangements Markov kernel is a valid common version for the entire family 0≤p≤1: it gives the correct point mass on the one observed group at each boundary and assigns permissible versions on its unobserved groups. Define the joint probability mass function there by the original product of the one-trial Bernoulli probability mass functions, or use the limiting convention 00=1 in the compact formula.
The sample mean T/n is an unbiased estimator of p and retains the sufficient statistic because n is known. By contrast, X1​ is also an unbiased estimator of p but, for n≥2, is not sufficient: the conditional success probability of the independent X2​ given X1​ is still p. Thus unbiasedness does not imply sufficiency.
Sufficiency also does not imply completeness of a statistic. For n≥2, the full-data sufficient statistic X admits the nonzero function g(X)=X1​−X2​ with expectation zero for every p. Nor does minimality imply completeness of a statistic: for n=2 and the restricted statistical model p∈{1/4,3/4}, T is a minimal sufficient statistic since the likelihood ratio P3/4​(X=x)/P1/4​(X=x)=32t−2 distinguishes its three values. Yet g(0)=3,g(1)=−5,g(2)=3 has expectation (27−30+3)/16=0 at both parameter values and is never zero. Changing the parameter family can change completeness of a statistic even while preserving sufficiency.

Sufficient statistic OurBigBook.com
A sufficient statistic allows the observed likelihood function to be stored through a shorter record, up to a parameter-independent factor. For the Bernoulli sample sum as a sufficient statistic, write
Lx​(p)=pt(1−p)n−t,Lt​(p)=(tn​)pt(1−p)n−t=(tn​)Lx​(p).
(64)
The second likelihood function belongs to the observed count; the first belongs to the observed sequence. Their absolute values differ by the binomial coefficient, but their likelihood ratios between any two interior parameter values agree. A maximum-likelihood estimator can therefore use just (n,t).
This compression discards which arrangement actually occurred. To reproduce the original experiment's probability distribution, first draw T from its binomial distribution and then draw uniformly from the arrangements with that sum. The second step is independent of p, so it supplies no additional evidence about p. It does not recover the particular discarded sequence. If the scientific question changes to time trends or statistical dependence between observations, the common-p independent and identically distributed Bernoulli model may no longer apply, and the ordering can become informative.

Each partition is maximal: splitting one of its two-point cells singles out a point whose probability depends on θ. (68)
The statistical parameter can enter gθ​ only through θ and the observed T(x). [ref]
For discrete data, take counting measure; for ordinary continuous data, take Lebesgue measure. Independence, identical sampling laws, smooth dependence on θ, and a fixed positive support of a probability distribution are not requirements of this theorem. Parameter-dependent support must nevertheless be included in fθ​, usually through an indicator function, and must fit the displayed factorization. The sufficient statistic for a symmetric uniform sample illustrates exactly this: its indicator function depends on the unknown scale through the observed absolute maximum. The null sets in the theorem concern versions of densities; the factors are not generally themselves normalized probability distributions.
For a discrete sample space, the cancellation behind the theorem is particularly transparent. On a group with positive probability, factorization gives
Pθ​(X=x∣T=t)=∑z:T(z)=t​h(z)h(x)1{T(x)=t}​​.
(69)
Conversely, multiply a common conditional probability mass function by Pθ​(T=T(x)) to obtain the required factorization. For continuous data, a sum over a group is not a density integral over the original Lebesgue measure: the group may have measure zero. Use the regular conditional distribution formulation and the Fisher-Neyman factorization theorem instead of that discrete calculation.

Sample mean sufficiency depends on the model (X=n−1∑i​Xi​)

Words: 146
Sufficient statistic OurBigBook.com
For the normal sample sum with known variance, assume independent and identically distributed Xi​∼N(μ,σ2) with fixed known variance σ2>0. The joint probability density factors as
fμ​(x)=h(x)(2πσ2)−n/2exp[−2σ2∑i​xi2​​]​​gμ​(∑i​xi​)exp[σ2μ∑i​xi​​−2σ2nμ2​]​​.
(70)
The Fisher-Neyman factorization theorem proves that the sum, and hence the sample mean, is a sufficient statistic for μ. Its remaining deviations Xi​−X have a joint Gaussian law independent of μ and are independent of X. If both μ and σ2 are unknown, the sample mean alone loses information about variance; the pair (∑i​Xi​,∑i​Xi2​) is sufficient for the full statistical parameter.
A discrete counterexample shows why a sample mean is not automatically sufficient for arbitrary statistical models. Let X1​,X2​ be independent and identically distributed on {0,1,2} with
Pθ​(Xi​=0)=Pθ​(Xi​=2)=θ/2,Pθ​(Xi​=1)=1−θ,0<θ<1.
(71)
Each observation has mean one. The arrangements (0,2),(1,1),(2,0) all give sample mean one, yet
Pθ​((X1​,X2​)=(1,1)∣X=1)=(1−θ)2+θ2/2(1−θ)2​.
(72)
This conditional probability is 18/19 at θ=1/4 and 2/11 at θ=3/4. The conditional distribution therefore still depends on the unknown statistical parameter: this sample mean is not a sufficient statistic. The useful reduction depends on the family of full-data laws, even when its mean stays fixed.

Linear least squares

Words: 62 Articles: 2
Probability and statistics OurBigBook.com
Linear least squares minimizes ∥Ax−b∥2 over a vector x. Its normal equations for linear least squares are ATAx=ATb; geometrically Ax is the orthogonal projection of b onto the range of A.

Linear least-squares projection

Words: 39 Articles: 1
Linear least squares OurBigBook.com
This is an orthogonal projection interpretation of linear least squares. The best affine predictor has slope covariance divided by predictor variance and intercept chosen to match means.

Schur complement covariance

Words: 15
Linear least-squares projection OurBigBook.com
The residual variance after projection onto one factor is Var(Y)−Cov(X,Y)2/Var(X), a covariance Schur complement.
